BC Centre for Disease Control — Extreme Heat Preparedness Guide (2026 update)

Extreme heat events are becoming more frequent in British Columbia. During the 2021 heat dome,
hundreds of people died, most of them older adults living alone in homes without cooling.

Who is most at risk
- Older adults, especially those over 60
- People who live alone
- People with chronic conditions such as heart disease, diabetes or schizophrenia
- People who use substances
- Infants and young children
- People who are pregnant
- People with limited mobility

Before the heat
- Identify the coolest room in your home. Basements are often cooler.
- Buy a thermometer to monitor indoor temperature.
- Set up a buddy system to check on people at risk.
- Know where your nearest cooling centre is.
- Shade windows with blinds or curtains; exterior shading is more effective.
- If you have an air conditioner, make sure it works before summer.

During a heat warning
- Indoor temperatures above 31 C are dangerous for people at risk.
- Spend time in a cool place: an air-conditioned building, a library, a mall.
- Close windows and blinds during the day; open them at night if it is cooler outside.
- Drink plenty of water, even if you are not thirsty.
- Take a cool shower or bath, or sit with your feet in cool water.
- Wear loose, light clothing.
- Fans alone will not prevent heat illness when it is very hot.

Signs of heat illness
- Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, headache, fast breathing.
- Heat stroke: high body temperature, confusion, fainting, no sweating. Call 911.

After the heat
- Continue to check on vulnerable people; effects can be delayed.
- Report problems with building cooling to your landlord or strata.

For more information visit the BCCDC website or call HealthLinkBC at 8-1-1.

Screens, Sleep and the Second-Grade Brain
By a pediatric sleep researcher, Parents Weekly

When children turn seven, many families loosen screen rules. Homework
is light, siblings have tablets, and evening shows feel harmless. But a
growing body of research suggests the hour before bed matters more than
the total hours in the day.

In a 2025 study of 1,200 children aged 6 to 9, those who used a screen
in the 60 minutes before lights-out fell asleep an average of 19 minutes
later than those who did not. The effect was strongest for handheld
devices held close to the face, and weakest for a shared TV in the
living room.

The researchers point to three mechanisms:

1. Light. Blue-weighted light from screens delays melatonin release,
   especially in children, whose lenses let through more short-wave
   light than adults'.
2. Arousal. Games and short-form video are built to keep attention;
   a calm documentary was far less disruptive than a game.
3. Displacement. Screen time pushes out the wind-down routines,
   such as baths, reading and talking, that signal bedtime.

What helped? Families who set a fixed screens-off time, moved devices
out of the bedroom and replaced the last half hour with reading saw
sleep onset return to normal within two weeks. Total weekday screen
time mattered less than timing once it stayed under two hours.

Weekend effects were smaller but real: late Saturday screens shifted
Sunday bedtimes and made Monday mornings harder.

The author's advice is simple. Pick a screens-off time an hour before
bed and keep it every night, including weekends. Charge devices in the
kitchen. Keep the TV in a shared room. And if a child protests, offer
a choice between two books rather than a negotiation about minutes.

None of this means screens are harmful in themselves, the author adds.
The evidence points to when, not whether.

(Parents Weekly, September 2026)

Open Banking in Canada: What the Consumer-Driven Banking Act Means for Fintechs

After years of consultation, Canada's framework for consumer-driven
banking is moving from policy to implementation. The federal
government has named the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC)
as the oversight body, and the first phase focuses on read access:
letting consumers share their account and transaction data with
accredited third parties through secure APIs instead of screen
scraping.

What changes for fintechs

1. Accreditation. Any company that wants to receive data must be
   accredited. Requirements include security standards, insurance,
   complaint handling and a Canadian presence.
2. Common technical standard. Banks and fintechs will use a single
   API standard, expected to be based on FDX. This should end the
   patchwork of bank-specific integrations.
3. Liability. The framework sets out who pays when something goes
   wrong. In most cases, the party at fault is liable, and consumers
   are protected from losses they did not cause.
4. Screen scraping. Once the framework is live, credential-based
   scraping is expected to be phased out.

What is not in phase one

Write access, or 'payment initiation', is deferred to a second phase.
That means fintechs cannot yet trigger payments from a consumer's
bank account through the framework. Many in the industry had hoped
both would arrive together, and payments companies argue that the
real value lies in write access.

Timeline

The government expects the first accredited participants to go live
in 2026, with the largest banks required to participate first and
smaller institutions following. Industry groups warn the timeline is
tight.

Why it matters

For small businesses, read access could speed up lending decisions
and bookkeeping. For payments companies, the bigger shift comes with
write access, which could make account-to-account payments a
real alternative to cards.

(Fintech Weekly North, September 2026)

Ontario Classroom Cellphone and Device Policy: What Parents Need to Know (2026-27)

Starting this school year, all publicly funded schools in Ontario
must follow the updated provincial policy on personal mobile devices.

Kindergarten to Grade 6
- Students must keep personal mobile devices, including phones
  and smartwatches with messaging, turned off and out of sight for
  the full school day, including recess and lunch.
- Devices may be used only with a teacher's direction for learning,
  for health and medical reasons, or for special education needs.

Grades 7 to 12
- Devices must be silent and out of sight during instructional time.
- Use during breaks is set by each school's code of conduct.
- Social media sites are blocked on school networks and devices.

Consequences
- Students who do not follow the rules will be asked to hand in the
  device to the office until the end of the day.
- Repeat issues are handled under the school's progressive
  discipline approach, and parents will be contacted.

Vaping and cannabis
- Schools will remove vaping products from students and notify
  parents. Repeat incidents may lead to suspension.

Communication with families
- Schools will share how families can reach students in an
  emergency, usually through the main office.

What parents can do
- Talk with your child about the rules before the first day.
- If your child wears a smartwatch for safety, check whether it can
  be set to a school mode with messaging disabled.

(Provincial education update, September 2026)

tl;dr in 3 bullets?

The Quiet Cost of Status Meetings

Most product teams don't decide to have too many meetings. They accumulate them.
A standup gets added during a crunch. A weekly sync is created for a launch and never removed.
A 'quick alignment' call becomes recurring because nobody wants to be the person to cancel it.

We surveyed 212 product managers across 40 companies about their calendars.
The median PM spent 14.5 hours a week in recurring meetings.
Of those hours, respondents said 38% were 'mostly status', meaning information that could have been written.
Only 21% of recurring meetings had been reviewed in the past six months.

The cost isn't only the hours. It's the fragmentation.
A PM with four 30-minute meetings spread across a morning has no block longer than 50 minutes.
Deep work, like writing a spec or analysing a funnel, needs 90 minutes or more to get going.
Teams with 'meeting-free mornings' reported spec turnaround 1.6x faster.

What worked for the teams we interviewed:
1. A quarterly meeting audit. Every recurring meeting must justify itself or be deleted.
2. Written status by default. Status goes in a doc or channel; meetings are for decisions.
3. Default lengths of 25 or 50 minutes, not 30 or 60.
4. A named owner for every recurring meeting, who must cancel it when it has no agenda.
5. Protecting one long block per day for each PM.

The pushback is predictable.
Managers worry that written updates get skimmed.
Engineers worry that decisions will happen in docs they never see.
Both concerns are real, and both are solved by the same thing: a clear place where decisions are recorded.

One head of product told us: 'We didn't cut meetings. We cut the meetings that were pretending to be documents.'

The teams that stuck with it saw a second-order effect.
When status moved to writing, the remaining meetings got better.
People came prepared, because there was finally time to prepare.

If you run a team, try one experiment this month: find your oldest recurring meeting and ask whether it still needs to exist.
If nobody can say what it decided last time, you have your answer.
